theme: Doctrinal Pause: Suffering and the Christian Life
summary: Why Christians suffer; suffering as conformity to Christ; hope amid affliction
readingInstruction: Read Romans 8:18-30, 1 Peter 4:12-19, and 2 Corinthians 4:7-18. These three passages are the New Testament’s most direct teaching on suffering in the Christian life. Read them side by side, and notice what each says about the purpose, the presence, and the end of suffering.
settingTheScene: Yesterday you thought about God’s sovereignty. Today you think about how Christians are to live under it. The book of Job asked why the righteous suffer, and the answer it gave was God himself. The New Testament adds the missing piece: the answer is the God who has suffered. Paul, Peter, and the others wrote as people who were being beaten, jailed, and persecuted. They are not theorizing. They are speaking from inside the experience.
observation: Paul says, “I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us” (Romans 8:18).
The whole creation “waits with eager longing” and “groans together in the pains of childbirth” (8:19-22).
We “who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons” (8:23).
“The Spirit helps us in our weakness…intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words” (8:26).
“For those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose” (8:28). The good is defined in verse 29: being “conformed to the image of his Son.”
Peter says, “Do not be surprised at the fiery trial when it comes upon you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you” (1 Peter 4:12).
“But rejoice insofar as you share Christ’s sufferings, that you may also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed” (4:13).
“Therefore let those who suffer according to God’s will entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good” (4:19).
Paul says, “We have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us” (2 Corinthians 4:7).
“For this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison” (4:17).
doctrinalFocus:
The Christian view of suffering differs from every other view in one important way: it centers on a suffering Savior. Other religions explain suffering as illusion, as karma, or as a mere fact of life. The Bible treats suffering as real, as an enemy, as part of a fallen world, and as something God himself has entered. Jesus “learned obedience through what he suffered” (Hebrews 5:8), and he is “a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief” (Isaiah 53:3). When you suffer, you are not alone.

The New Testament gives several reasons for the suffering of Christians, and it is important to keep them together. First, we suffer because of union with Christ. Paul says we are “fellow heirs with Christ, provided we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him” (Romans 8:17). To belong to Jesus is to share his path, which goes through the cross to glory. Second, suffering refines us. It produces endurance, character, and hope (Romans 5:3-5), and it is the means by which God conforms us to his Son (Romans 8:29). Third, suffering is a witness. Paul carries “the death of Jesus” in his body “so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our bodies” (2 Corinthians 4:10). Fourth, suffering is the groaning of a creation that is still waiting for its redemption. We live in the time between the first coming and the second, and all of creation feels it.

We must be careful not to turn any of these reasons into a rule that explains every case. This is exactly what Job’s friends did. Jesus said that a man’s blindness was not caused by his sin or his parents’ (John 9:3). Sometimes we simply do not know why. What we do know is that God has promised never to leave us, that he is working through everything for our good, and that suffering will end.

That promise is the content of Romans 8:28. It is often quoted as if it said that everything that happens is good. It does not. It says that God works all things together for good, and the good is defined: becoming like Christ and sharing in his glory. That is a much deeper kind of good than comfort. And the verses that follow seal it. Nothing can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:38-39).

The final piece is hope. Paul calls the affliction “light” and “momentary,” not because it is trivial but because he is weighing it against “an eternal weight of glory.” The scales are not even. The Christian does not deny the pain. He sets it against what is coming.
interpretation:
Each of the three passages tells you something different. In Romans 8, Paul puts our pain in a cosmic frame. It is part of a creation that groans and a Spirit that groans with us. He does not say that the pain is good. He says that it is not the end. The Spirit helps us pray when we have no words, and that is a mercy that Job did not have.

In 1 Peter, the stress is on not being surprised. Peter writes to believers who are facing persecution, and he tells them that this is normal. “Do not be surprised.” Many people come to faith expecting an easier life, and they are shaken when trouble comes. Peter says to expect the fiery trial, and to rejoice when you share Christ’s sufferings. He also gives a simple instruction for the sufferer: “entrust your soul to a faithful Creator while doing good” (4:19). The phrase “faithful Creator” answers God’s speeches in Job. The one who made the world is the one to trust with your soul.

In 2 Corinthians 4, Paul describes himself as a jar of clay. The treasure is the gospel, and the jar is his fragile, breakable body. The weakness is not a flaw in the plan. It is the plan, so that the power will clearly be God’s. He says that he is afflicted but not crushed, perplexed but not driven to despair, struck down but not destroyed (4:8-9). Each of the pairs is a picture of someone near the edge who is held.

Together the passages give a full portrait. Suffering is real and costly. It is not a sign that God has left us. It is used by God for good. It is temporary. And it is shared with Christ.
connection: Job’s story points forward to these New Testament passages. Where Job asked for a mediator, Paul says the Spirit intercedes for us. Where Job looked for a redeemer, Peter points to the faithful Creator who is also our Savior. Hebrews 12:1-3 tells us to look to Jesus, who endured the cross. James 1:2-4 and Revelation 21:4 complete the picture: trials now, and no more tears then.
application:
First, if you are suffering now, read Romans 8:18-30 slowly and ask God to help you hear it as a word to you. Identify one phrase that gives you hope.

Second, if you are not suffering, take time to pray for someone who is. Read 1 Peter 4 and ask how you can support a persecuted brother or sister.

Third, learn 2 Corinthians 4:16-17 by heart. It will be a help in your own dark days.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus that he suffered for you and with you.
Tell God where you are weak and ask him to show his strength.
Ask him to fix your eyes on what is unseen.
